title: Seventh commandment (CCC 2401–2449)
hook: don't steal, pay fair wages, share the earth's goods

segments.voice: Yesterday, chastity: the person whole, body and spirit in tune, no double life. Your line was whole, not divided.

In the back of a garage, behind the bikes, leans a ladder. It belongs to the neighbor. It was borrowed for one gutter job, a few summers ago, and it has quietly become part of the furniture. Nobody would call it stealing. Nobody would call it giving back, either. In Jericho, a rich tax collector climbs a tree to see Jesus pass, and before the day is over he's promising to pay back fourfold anyone he has cheated. The seventh commandment reaches from the ladder to the tax office.
screen: `A BORROWED LADDER IN THE GARAGE.` → `A TAX COLLECTOR IN A TREE.` → `PAYING IT BACK.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not steal." Four words, and the Catechism builds a whole picture of economic life on them. It starts with creation: God entrusted the earth and its resources to the common stewardship of humanity, and its goods are meant for the whole human race. Private property is legitimate; it secures freedom and dignity and helps people meet their needs. But owning something doesn't cancel that first purpose: what a person owns is held for their family and, in some way, for others too. Then theft, widened. Not only taking what isn't yours, but keeping things lent or found. Fraud in business. Unjust wages. Raising prices by exploiting someone's ignorance or hardship. Work done poorly. Tax evasion. Waste. The ladder in the garage belongs on that list. And it asks for repair: what was taken should be given back. That's Zacchaeus, whom you met up a tree in year one. He tells Jesus he'll give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold to anyone he has wronged, and Jesus answers that salvation has come to that house. A just wage, the Catechism says, is the legitimate fruit of work; withholding it can be a grave injustice. And it ends with love for the poor, quoting Gregory the Great, in paraphrase: when we give the poor what they need, we aren't giving them what's ours, but returning what's theirs. Theft, here, isn't only a hand in someone's pocket. It's anything that keeps the earth's goods from the people they were made for.
screen: `THE EARTH ENTRUSTED TO ALL.` · `THEFT, WIDENED.` · `ZACCHAEUS PAYS IT BACK.` · `FAIR WAGES, AND THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Think through the people whose work you'll use today, the driver, the server, the cashier, the voice on the help line, and picture one of them clearly, on their long shift. Decide what fair looks like for them, a better tip, a prompt payment, a real thank-you, and if anything borrowed is still in your house, when it goes back. If you pray, ask for a generous hand.
Seventh commandment. Thou shalt not steal: respect for others' goods, fair wages, honest work, repair of what was taken, and the earth's goods shared with all, especially the poor. Today's word.
Your line: goods are for all. Even the ladder in the garage can still go home. That's today.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught to make restitution for what they've taken, to pay and work fairly, and to give to the poor through almsgiving, parish collections and the works of mercy.

chat.says: Is keeping something I borrowed ages ago really stealing?
options: The Catechism counts keeping things lent or found as theft, and asks that what was taken be given back.
No. If the owner hasn't asked for it back within a year, the Catechism says it becomes yours.
Only if you meant to steal it at the start; borrowed things never fall under the commandment.
chat.meaning: The Catechism widens theft to keeping things lent or found, unjust wages and fraud, and asks for repair, as Zacchaeus restored fourfold.
